summary: Describes four existing implementations of SPIRITS-like services, which start in the telephone network and need interaction with Internet services.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo describes four systems that let a subscriber on a dial-up Internet connection see an incoming phone call on their computer and decide what to do with it, instead of having the call interrupt the connection. The four come from Korea Telecom, Lucent, NEC and Telia with Nortel. It is a survey of how each one works, written to give the SPIRITS working group something concrete to build on.

questions: how do pstn and internet systems work together
how does a pstn call reach an internet client
subtitle: Four systems that let someone on a dial-up line see an incoming phone call on their computer and decide what to do with it.

tldr.problem: The SPIRITS working group needed to know what already existed, so that the interfaces it defines would connect real systems rather than a paper design.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes four existing implementations of telephone-network-initiated Internet services, one each from Korea Telecom, Lucent Technologies, NEC and Telia in cooperation with Nortel Networks, using Internet Call Waiting as the common benchmark service.
tldr.outcome: All four support call waiting, three use SIP between the telephone network and the Internet, and all use Intelligent Network systems for the telephone side. The memo concludes they do not interoperate with each other, which is the gap the working group had to close.

today: RFC 2995 is an Informational survey of four implementations written to support the SPIRITS working group, and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. The memo records that the four systems did not interoperate with one another, which is the gap the working group was asked to close. It is read with RFC 2848, the PINT service protocol, and with the SPIRITS architecture in RFC 3136.

sections.title: What the Document Surveys
sections.content:
The document contains information relevant to the work of the Services in the PSTN/IN Requesting InTernet Services (SPIRITS) working group. It describes four existing implementations of SPIRITS-like services from Korea Telecom, Lucent Technologies, NEC, and Telia in cooperation with Nortel Networks. SPIRITS-like services are those that originate in the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) and necessitate the interaction of the Internet and the PSTN.

The service invariably supported by the implementations examined is Internet Call Waiting (ICW). With ICW, service subscribers who are using their telephone lines for Internet access can be notified of incoming voice calls and can specify how to handle the calls over the same telephone lines.

The memo first gives a detailed description of the ICW service, then discusses each of the four implementations, and ends with security considerations, the conclusion and references. It notes that even though the term SPIRITS server is used throughout, it has no universal meaning: its connotation depends on the context and varies from implementation to implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo is a survey of four systems that already existed, written so the working group could design interfaces that real equipment would use. It also warns that the same term means different things in each system.

sections.title: The Internet Call Waiting Service
sections.content:
Internet call waiting is the single service specifically supported by all the implementations in question. It enables a subscriber engaged in an Internet dial-up session to be notified of an incoming call to the very same telephone line that is being used for the Internet connection, to specify the desirable treatment of the call, and to have the call handled as specified.

The features below are those supported by at least one of the implementations. Incoming call notification shows the subscriber a pop-up dialog box on the PC without any effect on the telephone line that the modem is using; the box may display the calling party number, the calling party name and the calling time, and displaying the name or number requires the caller name or number delivery feature to be available.

Once informed of the incoming call, the subscriber has options for handling it: accepting the call over the PSTN line, which terminates the Internet connection; accepting it over the Internet using Voice over IP; rejecting it; playing a pre-recorded message to the calling party and disconnecting the call; forwarding the call to voice mail; or forwarding it to another number. If the subscriber fails to respond within a certain period after the dialog box has been displayed, the call can be rejected or handled in the way the subscriber pre-defined.

Automatic incoming call disposition removes the real-time intervention. The subscriber pre-defines a default disposition for general calls, for example redirection to voice mail, and can define customised dispositions for calls from specific numbers, storing that information in a profile. With this in place the subscriber is not presented the call but can examine the treatment and outcome of the call from the caller log. The feature also covers calls from private or unpublished numbers.

Two further features complete the list. Multiple call handling lets several calls that arrive during call disposition processing be notified one by one. Call logging keeps a detailed log of the calls processed during the service, typically recording the incoming call date and time, the calling party number, the calling party name and the call disposition.
sections.plainLanguage: The subscriber gets a pop-up box showing who is calling and when. From there the call can be answered on the phone line, answered over the Internet as voice, rejected, answered with a recorded message, sent to voice mail, or sent to another number. The subscriber can also set rules in advance so calls are handled without asking, and keep a log of what happened.

sections.title: Korea Telecom's Implementation
sections.content:
Korea Telecom's implementation supports most of the features in Section 2, the major exception being receiving the incoming call over the Internet using voice over IP. It also supports flexible activation: the service is activated or de-activated automatically when an Internet dial-up connection is set up, and the subscriber can de-activate it manually when call notification is not wanted during the session and activate it when needed.

The architecture mixes legacy telephone network elements with two new ones. The Service Switching Point (SSP), Service Control Point (SCP) and Intelligent Peripheral (IP) are legacy PSTN Intelligent Network elements based on IN CS-1, while the ICW Server System and the ICW Client System are new elements installed in the Internet domain. The SSP performs the Service Switching Function and Call Control Function; when it detects that the called party is busy it queries the SCP and processes the call under the SCP's control. The SCP performs the Service Control Function and the Service Data Function, and also performs the Service Control Gateway Function for protocol interworking between the telephone network and the Internet: it translates the SIP message from the ICW Server into the service control interface message and back, and behaves as a SIP user agent. The IP holds the Service Resource Function, plays announcements to the calling party during the service, and records the calling party number or a voice message when the call is forwarded to voice mail.

The ICW Server System serves as a SIP proxy or redirect server for message routing between the ICW Client and the gateway function, and manages the connected clients. When a client sends a registration request, the server relays it to the SCP, waits for the result of authorisation, and registers the authorised subscriber in its database. It monitors the connection status of registered clients and de-activates the service as soon as a client de-activates it or terminates the Internet connection, and it manages the per-subscriber profiles and the log of call processing results. The ICW Client System is an application on the subscriber's PC, launched when the PC is powered on. It monitors the Internet connection status, sends a registration request to the gateway function through the ICW Server, and thereafter notifies the server periodically of the connection status. It also pops up the dialog box and, once the subscriber has chosen an option, sends that choice to the SCP. Packet filtering firewalls sit between the ICW server and the clients, and between the gateway function and the ICW server.

The Internet side uses the PINT Service Protocol 1.0, developed in the IETF PINT working group for invoking telephone services from an IP network, which specifies a set of enhancements to SIP 2.0 and SDP. The REGISTER method informs the SCP of the connection status of a subscriber: the client sends the IP address of the PC and the subscriber's phone number when the connection is first made, the server relays the information to the SCP, which updates its database if the subscriber is authorised, and the registration acknowledgement travels back the same way. After that the client sends a REGISTER request to the server periodically, at a pre-defined interval such as 20 seconds, to indicate its connection status, and that request is not relayed to the SCP. The INVITE method notifies the client of an incoming call, ACK confirms receipt of the final responses, BYE terminates the session and its Subject header carries the result of the desired disposition, and CANCEL withdraws an INVITE when the calling party releases the call before the called party responds.

The client answers an INVITE with one of a small set of status codes: 100 Trying, 200 OK to accept the call, 303 See Other to forward the call to another number, 380 Alternative Service to forward the call to voice mail, and 603 Decline to reject the call. In each case the ICW Server relays the choice to the gateway function, which translates it to the SCP's internal interface, and the service control function then instructs the switch to complete or reroute the call. The telephone side uses the KT INAP V1.0, based on ITU-T INAP CS-1 with two INAP CS-2 messages added, PromptAndReceiveMessage and EraseMessage, for recording the voice message.
sections.plainLanguage: When the dial-up connection starts, the program on the PC registers its address and phone number with the telephone network's control point, and keeps telling it that it is online. When a call arrives, the telephone network asks that control point what to do, and the control point sends an invitation to the PC, which shows the pop-up box. The subscriber's answer travels back the same way, and the telephone network carries out the call.

sections.title: The Other Three Implementations
sections.content:
Lucent's Online Communications Center (OCC) is an Intelligent Network based platform whose basic components are the OCC Server and the OCC Client. The server interacts with the PSTN entities over a secure intranet using plain-text SIP messages, and with the PC client using encrypted SIP messages. Its run-time environment consists of two multi-threaded processes responsible for call registration and call notification. The architecture places the OCC Server on a Compact Service Node, with a service package application on the Service Control Point; the central office is simply provisioned to query the Service Control Point when a termination attempt is directed at the subscriber's number, so no central office software specific to OCC has to be installed. The subscriber's record in the real-time database holds the directory number, the PIN, the IP address, a flag saying whether a call notification is in progress, a session key and a language identifier. The server listens for SIP REGISTER messages from clients and SIP INVITE messages from the control point on distinct TCP/IP ports, opens a new socket to each client for each notification session, and handles encryption and decryption of the messages exchanged with the client, including the session-specific keys.

NEC's implementation is also based on Intelligent Network elements, with a SPIRITS server and an ICW client. The line is primed for the service when the customer dials the ISP access number with a special activation code prefix, and the service is activated when the user opens a secured session from the ICW client to the SPIRITS server, so the server knows the relationship between the line and the PC. When a call arrives at a busy Internet line, the switching point triggers the service and the SCP, acting as the SPIRITS client, tells the SPIRITS server that a call is terminating to a busy Internet line, including the caller ID, the calling line identify restriction status and the directory number of the busy line. The SPIRITS server checks that an ICW session has been established, the user receives a pop-up with the calling name and number if available, and their choice of answering, sending to voice mail, forwarding elsewhere or ignoring is sent back through the SPIRITS server, which instructs the PSTN via the SCP. NEC is the one implementation that does not use SIP: it uses a proprietary protocol, though it has a plan to support SIP together with the extensions for SPIRITS services.

Telia and Nortel's system is designed for services that execute before the end-to-end media session is established, such as call transfer and number portability, call waiting and call offering, call screening and don't disturb, and automatic call distribution and 800 services. Prototypes for online incoming call disposition and automatic incoming call disposition were developed to prove the concept. The services run on top of SIP redirect servers, and a new network element, the Service Control Gateway, hides the true situation from the services: it converts network-specific call control signalling to SIP messages and back, behaving as a SIP user agent towards the services and as a network-specific service control node in the network where the call is being set up. It handles protocol conversions but not address translation, which is left to a regular SIP server to keep the gateway simple. In the memo's number portability example, the INAP message carrying the number query is converted by the gateway into a SIP INVITE for a redirect server, which answers 404 Not Found for a number that is not ported and 301 Moved Permanently with a routing number for one that is; the gateway turns the answer back into a message for the telephone network. Running the redirect server in proxy mode turns it into a service router that can relay number queries to any redirect-server-based service reachable over IP, so the same service can work across several telephone networks.
sections.plainLanguage: Lucent and NEC both keep the telephone network's control point in charge, and NEC is the one that uses its own protocol rather than SIP. Telia and Nortel take a different approach: a gateway converts each telephone network's own signalling into SIP, so that one service written in SIP can work in several telephone networks at once.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says the SPIRITS security requirements are essentially the same as those for PINT: protection of the PSTN from attacks from the Internet, peer entity authentication so a communicating entity can prove its identity to another in the network, authorisation and access control to verify whether a network entity is allowed to use a network resource, confidentiality to avoid disclosure of information such as the end user profile and data without the permission of its owner, and non-repudiation to account for all operations in case of doubt or dispute.

The implementations examined have met these requirements with different means, mostly firewalls and encryption. The Lucent architecture passes plain-text SIP over a secure intranet between the PSTN entities and encrypted SIP to the PC client, with packet filtering firewalls between the ICW server and the clients and between the gateway function and the ICW server. The Telia and Nortel architecture uses the security mechanisms available to ordinary SIP services, implemented as they would be in a pure SIP network, and imposes no additional security considerations of its own. The memo does note that interconnecting two different networks is a general security issue: the gateways must include mechanisms that prevent destructive service control signalling from one network reaching the other, for example a firewall-type mechanism that can block a denial-of-service attack from an Internet user towards the PSTN.
sections.plainLanguage: The requirements are the same as for PINT: keep the telephone network safe from the Internet, authenticate both ends, check who may use which resource, keep user data private, and be able to account for what happened. The four systems meet them differently, mostly with firewalls and encryption.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.content:
The memo has provided information relevant to the development of inter-networking interfaces between the PSTN and the Internet for supporting SPIRITS services, by describing four existing implementations of SPIRITS-like services. Surveying them, it makes three observations. The ICW service plays the role of a benchmark service: all four implementations can support ICW, with three specifically designed for it. SIP is used in most of the implementations as the base communications protocol between the PSTN and the Internet; NEC's implementation is the only exception, using a proprietary protocol, though it has a plan to support SIP together with the extensions for SPIRITS services. All implementations use IN-based solutions for the PSTN part.

It is clear that not all pre-SPIRITS implementations interoperate with each other. It is also clear that not all SIP-based implementations interoperate with each other, given that they do not support the same version of SIP. It is a task of the SPIRITS working group to define the inter-networking interfaces that will support interoperation of the future implementations of SPIRITS services.
sections.plainLanguage: Call waiting was the common ground, SIP was nearly the common language, and the telephone side was always software-controlled. What was missing was agreement: the four systems could not talk to each other, and that was the work the working group took on.

items.title: Incoming call notification
items.text: A pop-up on the PC showing the caller's number, name and time, without touching the modem line.

items.title: Online disposition
items.text: Accept on the line or over the Internet, reject, play a message, send to voice mail, or forward.

items.title: Automatic disposition
items.text: Handling defined in advance, with separate rules for particular calling numbers.

items.title: Multiple call handling
items.text: Several calls arriving at once are notified one by one.

items.title: Call logging
items.text: A log of the date, time, calling party and what was done with each call.
